While running the beta, we highly recommend joining our #beta channel on
the Home Assistant Discord chat! 💬 Most developers and beta
testers are in this channel during the beta period to share experiences, ideas,
and iterate over new features, fine-tuning them before the final release.
It’s a really fun place to hang out. 😎

Reporting issues: As this is a beta test, you might encounter unexpected

Issues introduced in the beta are processed with priority. 🔝

A huge thank you to all the contributors who made this release possible! And a special shout-out to @abb848 and @bramkragten who helped write the release notes this release. ❤️

Welcome to the Marketplace

For years, the community has built custom integrations A custom integration is an integration that has been created by someone from the Home Assistant community and has been published for others to use at their own risk. Custom integrations are not supported by the Home Assistant project. They are not reviewed or tested by the Home Assistant development team and thus may negatively impact the stability of your Home Assistant instance. An example of a custom integration is the Spook integration., dashboard cards, themes, and templates for Home Assistant. People found them through HACS, the Home Assistant Community Store. With this release, HACS becomes part of Home Assistant as the new Marketplace.

The Marketplace brings the existing HACS experience into Home Assistant and the regular release process. It works with every installation type, including Home Assistant Container Home Assistant Container is a standalone container-based installation of Home Assistant Core. Any OCI compatible runtime can be used, but the documentation focus is on Docker. [Learn more], without manually downloading or unpacking files. Everything in the Marketplace is free, and that will not change.

Browse and install

You can find the Marketplace under Settings > Marketplace. It comes with Home Assistant, so there is nothing to set up. As an administrator, you can browse the catalog and install integrations, dashboard cards, themes, and templates. You do not need a GitHub account to install or update projects.

Installing a new integration Integrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] got shorter, too. In HACS, you downloaded it, restarted Home Assistant, went to Devices & services, and searched for it again to set it up. In the Marketplace, you select Install, and you land straight in its setup flow, without a restart. Updates still need a restart for now.

The page of each project now shows more than its README: how often it was downloaded, its stars on GitHub, and the Home Assistant version it requires, so you know what you’re getting into before you install.

Every project you install gets an “update entity” An update entity is an entity that indicates if an update is available for a device or service. [Learn more], so updates show up under Settings > Updates, next to the updates of Home Assistant itself. After an update, a repair tells you when a restart is needed, and can restart Home Assistant for you.

The first time you open the Marketplace, it shows a notice. Everything in the Marketplace is made by the community. It is not tested, audited, or supported by the Home Assistant project, and it runs inside your Home Assistant. Read the notice, select I understand the risks and agree, and you’re in. Browsing works before that. Installing and updating does not.

The Marketplace adds several improvements:

Group the Browse and Installed lists by status, type, or source. Home Assistant remembers your grouping.

Filter by source to distinguish the community catalog from custom repositories.

Select multiple repositories on the Installed tab and uninstall them at once.

Skipped updates no longer keep a repository at the top of the list or count in the update badge. A new release makes the update available again.

Search, filters, and sorting are saved in the URL, so you can share a link to a specific Marketplace view.

Integrations show their brand images before you install them.

Custom repositories

Name it once, Home Assistant adds the context

Name a thing once, and Home Assistant makes sure it makes sense everywhere. That is the idea behind how entities An entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] are named from this release on, and it has been more than four years in the making. You give an entity its own name, like “Temperature”. Home Assistant knows which device it belongs to, and in which area that device lives, so it can add that context where it helps. By default, that is the name of the device: the “Temperature” of a “Thermostat” in the “Bedroom” shows up as “Thermostat Temperature”. Where you want more, a card can add the area too, like “Bedroom Thermostat Temperature”.

Naming has been a topic in the community for years, with threads like “How do you name your devices?” and “Naming strategies for entities?”, all looking for a system that keeps a growing home readable.

It’s time to let those systems go. You shouldn’t need a strategy to make sense of the information in Home Assistant. Home Assistant should give you the context you need, at the moment you need it. Now you rename the device, and every entity on it follows. Entities you renamed, and entities you never touched, get their context the same way.

You see this in dashboards, settings, the activity and logbook, the voice assistant settings, and the apps. The same name, in the same structure, everywhere you look.

A few things to know:

Renaming an entity only renames the entity. If you want to change the name of the device, rename the device. If an entity represents the main function of its device, turn on Main entity of the device in its settings, and it goes by the name and the area of the device.

Devices with multiple parts, like a power strip, now get a device A device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. per part, each with its own name and area An area in Home Assistant is a logical grouping of devices and entities that represents a room or space in your home, such as the living room, kitchen, or garage. [Learn more]. These are called child devices. A child device inherits the area of its parent, until you give it one of its own. Integrations are moving to them one by one, starting with the multi-channel switches in Tuya.

Your own names are kept. Home Assistant migrates names you set. If an entity’s displayed name changes, the old name remains an alias for voice assistants. For example, “turn on the ceiling light” continues to work.

Templates: The friendly_name attribute is planned for deprecation. Use entity_name(), device_name(), and area_name() to build the name you need.

Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more], and dashboards keep working.

articles.title: Home Assistant 2026.11 brings community projects into the Marketplace
articles.dek: Today’s release brings HACS into Home Assistant, adds exclusions to automation targets, and opens camera talkback through Matter and Reolink.
body: Home Assistant 2026.11 arrives today with the Marketplace built in. The successor to HACS lets administrators browse and install community integrations, dashboard cards, themes and templates from Settings, including on Container installations. Catalogue downloads need no GitHub account, and a newly installed integration opens its setup flow without restarting Home Assistant. Existing HACS installations migrate automatically, keeping installed projects, custom repositories and update entities.

Updates to community projects still require a restart, and adding a custom repository still needs a GitHub connection. Bringing the catalogue into Home Assistant does not turn its contents into officially supported software: projects run inside the installation and remain unaudited by the Home Assistant project. Franck Nijhof’s release notes credit HACS founder Joakim Sørensen and the project’s maintainers for making the transition possible.

Automation targets gain exclusions, so a rule can act on the ground floor while leaving out the kitchen. Those selections are recalculated each time the rule runs, including devices added later. Matter 1.5 cameras also gain live video and snapshots. An optional Two-way audio feature in Labs adds a talk button for supported Matter and Reolink cameras; it requires HTTPS, and Reolink cameras must use RTSP streaming.

Before upgrading, Z-Wave users need Z-Wave JS server 3.11.0 or later: at least version 1.9.0 of the Z-Wave JS app, or Z-Wave JS UI 11.24.2. Older Telegram notification actions are also removed; affected automations need the Telegram bot integration’s notification entities or its own actions. The release notes list the remaining integration-specific changes to check.

articles.title: Home Assistant shows which access tokens are still being used
articles.dek: The profile lists each token’s latest use and connecting address, helping owners identify forgotten credentials.
body: Home Assistant shows when a long-lived access token was last used and the address it connected from. The information appears beside the token in the user’s profile, helping an owner distinguish an active script or integration from a credential they may no longer need.

Usage is recorded when a token authenticates an HTTP request or a WebSocket connection. Older tokens show no usage line until they are used again, avoiding a misleading creation date. This is a latest-use record rather than a complete access log, and inactivity does not make a token expire.

articles.title: ESPHome stops voice satellites answering their own replies
articles.dek: The microphone waits for a delayed response to finish before listening for the next turn.
body: ESPHome corrects a conversation loop in which a voice satellite starts listening before its own spoken reply has begun. The satellite could transcribe that reply as a new request and answer itself, rather than waiting for the person to speak.

Satellites using ESPHome’s media player wait up to fifteen seconds for speech to start and keep the microphone closed while the response plays. If playback never starts, they skip the follow-up turn. Tests on Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition covered short and long replies; neither was recorded as a fresh request with the correction. This is psewar’s first ESPHome contribution.

articles.title: Home Assistant keeps SmartThings device updates from freezing
articles.dek: Renewing the connection’s token prevents a healthy-looking stream from silently going stale.
body: Home Assistant keeps SmartThings device readings moving when its access token expires. A connection could continue receiving keepalive messages while actual device events stopped, leaving readings frozen or a device marked unavailable until someone reloaded the integration.

The integration checks the token every minute and renews it through its existing sign-in handling. Failed renewals are retried, and a rejected refresh token prompts authentication again. Paol0B makes a first contribution to Home Assistant Core with the correction.

articles.title: Matter.js stops devices inheriting a controller’s access rights
articles.dek: The correction targets connections that use special permission tags to grant access.
body: Matter.js corrects access checks on secure connections it initiates. Where special permission tags are configured, a remote device could inherit rights intended for the local controller while losing rights granted to its own identity.

Ingo Fischer makes the connection use the tags from the remote device’s signed certificate, including when reconnecting through a saved session. Older saved sessions with potentially incorrect tags are discarded so the devices establish a fresh secure connection. The correction applies to applications built on Matter.js; most installations do not configure these tags.

articles.dek: Player setup can reconnect after unpairing or switching off guest access.
body: Music Assistant lets owners set up a Sendspin player again after unpairing it or disabling guest access. Previously, the settings promised that the device would reconnect by itself, but offered no way to pair it again.

Starting setup contacts the device so it can be paired with its code, or used without pairing if guest access remains enabled. Clearer messages distinguish this from a device taken over by another music server, which Music Assistant can reclaim by starting playback.

articles.title: Inovelli’s stable presence-switch update changes automation reporting
articles.dek: VZW32-SN firmware 2.4 turns off a duplicate occupancy report by default.
body: Z-Wave JS’s firmware catalogue moves Inovelli VZW32-SN firmware 2.4 to the stable channel. Owners updating from the previous stable firmware need to check automations using the “Person in Reporting Area” value: it no longer updates automatically by default.

Inovelli recommends using the motion notification instead, because the extra report repeats that information and adds network traffic every few seconds. Owners who need the old report can enable it with parameter 107 set to 2.

articles.title: Theme authors gain a reference that follows Home Assistant’s code
articles.dek: The contributor site lists default values for light and dark themes and checks for removed settings.
body: Home Assistant’s contributor site adds a theme-variable reference with defaults for light and dark modes. Aidan Timson replaces the manually maintained frontend wiki list with a page generated from the theme source, alongside selected component settings such as dashboard gaps and editor colours.

The weekly update workflow refreshes the page and lists added or removed variables for review. Component settings still need a curated list, but the generator checks whether the referenced code continues to use them.
